Hippothous led the tribes of the spear-fighting Pelasgians, who lived in deep-soiled Larissa — Hippothous and Pylaeus, of the line of Ares, the two sons of Pelasgian Lethus, son of Teutamus.

Acamas and the warrior Peirous led the Thracians, all that the strong-flowing Hellespont closes within. Euphemus led the spear-armed Cicones, son of Troezenus, son of Ceas, cherished of Zeus. Pyraechmes led the Paeonians with their curved bows, from far-off Amydon, from the broad waters of the Axius — the Axius, whose stream spreads the loveliest water over the earth.

The Paphlagonians were led by the strong heart of Pylaemenes, from the land of the Eneti, where the wild mules are bred — the men who held Cytorus and lived around Sesamus, in their famous homes by the river Parthenius, in Cromna and Aegialus and lofty Erithini. The Halizones were led by Odius and Epistrophus, from far-off Alybe, the birthplace of silver. The Mysians were led by Chromis and Ennomus, reader of birds — but his bird-lore did not ward off the black death; he went down at the hands of the swift-footed grandson of Aeacus, in the river, where Achilles cut down other Trojans too.

Phorcys led the Phrygians, with godlike Ascanius, from far Ascania, both of them straining for the fight. The Maeonians were led by Mesthles and Antiphus, the two sons of Talaemenes, born to him by the Gygaean lake — they who led the Maeonians, born under Mount Tmolus. Nastes led the Carians, men of a strange tongue, who held Miletus and the leafy mountain of Phthires, the streams of the Maeander, and the steep crests of Mycale. Amphimachus and Nastes led them — Nastes and Amphimachus, the splendid children of Nomion. Amphimachus came to the war decked in gold, like a girl — the fool; the gold did nothing to keep off his bitter end. He went down at the hands of the swift-footed grandson of Aeacus, in the river, and the great fighter Achilles carried off his gold. Sarpedon and faultless Glaucus led the Lycians, from far-off Lycia, from the eddying Xanthus.

When the companies had formed up, each behind its own captain, the Trojans came on with a din and a clamor, like birds — like the cranes that scream overhead when winter and the rains drive them south over the streams of Ocean, carrying death and ruin to the Pygmy men, and they fall on them out of the dawn with a murderous quarrel. But the Greeks came on in silence, breathing fury, their hearts set on standing by one another.

As the south wind drapes the mountaintops in mist — no friend to the shepherd, but better than night to the thief, for a man can see no farther than the cast of a stone — so the dust rose in clouds under their feet as they crossed the plain at speed.

When the two armies had closed to within reach of each other, Alexandros stepped out ahead of the Trojan line to fight as their champion. A leopard's skin hung from his shoulders, and his curved bow, and his sword; and he shook two bronze-tipped spears and dared the best of the Greeks to come and face him man to man. Menelaus saw him striding out before the ranks and his heart leaped — the way a lion's does, starved, when it lights on the carcass of a great goat or an antlered stag and tears into it on the spot, though hounds and quick young hunters press in on it. So Menelaus rejoiced when he set eyes on Alexandros, for he thought: now I pay back the man who wronged me. Down from his chariot he sprang in his armor.

But Alexandros, husband of lovely-haired Helen, saw Menelaus come forward, and his courage broke. He shrank back into the ranks of his own men to save his life. As a man jumps back when he comes on a snake in a mountain hollow — a shudder takes him, he goes pale, he gives ground — so Alexandros, struck with terror at the sight of the son of Atreus, ducked back into the press of the proud Trojans.

Hector saw it, and turned on him with scorn: "Paris — you cursed, pretty Paris, you woman-crazed seducer, all looks and lies — better you had never been born, or had died unmarried. I'd take that, far rather than have you stand here a disgrace, a thing men look at sideways. You can hear the Greeks laughing now — they thought our champion would be a great fighter, because he's a fine-looking man, and they've found out he has no nerve and no fight in him at all. Was it this same weakness in you when you gathered your loyal crews and sailed across the sea, mixed with foreigners, and carried off a beautiful woman from a far country, a bride married into a nation of spearmen — and brought down ruin on your father, on your city, on your whole people, joy to your enemies, and shame on your own head? And now you won't stand and face Menelaus? You'd learn fast enough what kind of man it is whose wife you took. Your lyre would do you no good then, and neither would Aphrodite's gifts — your good looks, your fine hair — when you lay in the dust. The Trojans are too soft, or you'd have been stoned in a coat of rock long ago for the harm you've done them."

And Alexandros answered him: "Hector, that's a fair charge — I won't pretend it isn't. Your heart is like an axe a shipwright drives through a beam, and the man's own strength gives the stroke its weight — that's how hard the edge of your scorn cuts. But don't throw golden Aphrodite's gifts in my face. The gods' own gifts are not to be thrown away; no man takes them by wanting them — the gods give them where they please. Still, if you want me to fight, then sit the Trojans and the Greeks down, and put me in the middle with Menelaus, the two of us, to fight it out for Helen and all her wealth. Whichever of us wins, whoever proves the better man, let him take the woman and everything she owns and carry it home — and let the rest of you swear a binding peace, so that you Trojans go on living here in the rich land of Troy, and the Greeks sail home to Argos and the green country of Achaea."

Hector was glad to hear it. He went out into the no-man's-land between the armies, gripping his spear by the middle to hold his own men back, and they all sat down at his signal. But the Greeks kept aiming at him, loosing arrows and slinging stones, until Agamemnon, lord of men, shouted them down: "Hold — Greeks, hold! Don't shoot. Hector wants to speak."

They stopped, and held their fire, and fell quiet, and Hector spoke between the two armies: "Hear me, Trojans, and you Greeks. I bring the offer of Alexandros, the man this whole war began over. He asks both sides to lay their arms down on the ground, and he and Menelaus will fight, the two of them alone in the middle, for Helen and all her wealth. Whichever wins, whoever proves the better man, let him take the woman and everything she owns, and let the rest of us swear a binding peace."

He finished, and they all went still. Then Menelaus, who roars in battle, spoke up: "Now hear me too — for the wound is mine most of all. It's my belief the Greeks and the Trojans can part at last, after all the suffering you have borne for my quarrel, and for what Alexandros did to me. Whichever of us is fated to die, let him die — and let the rest of you be done with fighting. Bring two lambs — a white ram and a black ewe, one for the Sun and one for the Earth — and we'll bring a third for Zeus. And send for Priam, so the old king swears the oath himself; his sons are reckless men, not to be trusted, and the oaths of Zeus must not be made and broken. A young man's mind blows whichever way the wind goes, but where an old man takes part, he looks before and after, and weighs what will turn out best for both sides."

The Trojans and the Greeks were glad to hear it, hoping the war was finally over. They reined their chariots back into the lines, climbed down, and stripped off their armor, laying it on the ground; and the two armies came close, with only a little stretch of bare earth between them. Hector sent two runners to the city for the lambs, and to fetch Priam, and Agamemnon sent Talthybius back to the ships for the third lamb; and he did as the king commanded.

Meanwhile Iris came to white-armed Helen with the news, taking the shape of her sister-in-law — the wife of Antenor's son, for Helicaon had married Laodice, the loveliest of Priam's daughters. She found Helen in her chamber, weaving at a great purple web, working into the cloth the many battles that the Trojans and the Greeks had fought for her sake at the hands of Ares. Iris came close and said: "Come and see, dear girl — there's a strange thing happening out there. The Trojans and the Greeks were on the plain a moment ago, mad for the fight; now they've stopped. The war has gone silent. They're leaning on their shields with their spears stuck upright in the ground beside them. And Alexandros and Menelaus are going to fight for you, the two of them with the long spears — and you'll be called the wife of whichever man wins."

So the goddess spoke, and she set in Helen's heart a sweet longing for the husband she had left, and her city, and her parents. She threw a white veil over her head and hurried out of the chamber, the tears already coming, and not alone — two of her women went with her, Aithra, daughter of Pittheus, and wide-eyed Clymene. And quickly they came to the Scaean gates.

There the elders of the people sat by the Scaean gates — Priam, and Panthous, and Thymoetes, Lampus and Clytius and Hicetaon of the line of Ares, and the two wise ones, Ucalegon and Antenor. Too old now to fight, but fine speakers still, they sat on the tower like cicadas that perch in a tree and pour out their thin, delicate song through the wood. When they saw Helen coming toward the tower, they spoke low to one another, with wings in their words: "No shame, then, that the Trojans and the Greeks have borne so much, so long, for a woman like that. She is terribly like the deathless goddesses to look on. And yet — beautiful as she is, let her go home in the ships, and not be left here to bring grief on us, and on our children after us."

But Priam called her over to him: "Come here, dear child, and sit in front of me — you'll see your first husband, and your kinsmen, and your friends. I lay no blame on you. To my mind it is the gods who are to blame; it is they who brought this miserable war of the Greeks down on us. Now tell me: who is that huge man over there, that great and lordly Greek? There are taller men in that army by a head, but I have never laid eyes on one so handsome, so much a king to look at. Surely he is a king."

And Helen, radiant among women, answered him: "You are dear to me, and I hold you in awe, father of my husband. I wish a hard death had been my choice instead, when I followed your son here and left behind my marriage bed, my kinsmen, my one beloved daughter, and the dear friends of my girlhood. But that was not to be, and so I waste away in tears. Still, I'll tell you what you ask. That man is Agamemnon, son of Atreus, wide-ruling — a good king and a strong spearman both. And he was my own brother-in-law, shameless as I am — if that life was ever real."

The old man gazed at him in wonder and said: "Fortunate son of Atreus — born lucky, blessed by the gods. So many sons of the Greeks are under your command. I went once to Phrygia, the land of vines, and saw the great host of horsemen there, the people of Otreus and of godlike Mygdon, camped along the banks of the Sangarius. I was their ally, drawn up among them, the day the Amazons came against us, those women who fight like men. But even they were not so many as these bright-eyed Greeks."

Then the old man looked at Odysseus and asked: "Now tell me about that one, dear child. Who is he? He's shorter than Agamemnon by a head, but broader in the chest and across the shoulders. His armor lies on the ground, and he ranges along the front of the ranks like a ram — like a great thick-fleeced ram going up and down through a flock of white ewes."
And Helen, child of Zeus, answered: "That is Laertes' son, Odysseus, a man of many turns. He was raised in Ithaca, that rugged island, and there is no trick or scheme he does not know."

Wise Antenor took up her words: "Lady, what you say is true. Odysseus came here once, on an embassy for your sake, and Menelaus with him; I was their host and gave them welcome under my own roof, so I came to know both men, their bodies and their minds. When they stood up among the assembled Trojans, Menelaus was the broader-shouldered of the two; but when both sat, Odysseus had the more lordly presence. When they rose to make their case before us all, Menelaus spoke fluently, only a few words, but very clear and to the point — no man of many words, though he was the younger. But when Odysseus, the man of many turns, got up, he would stand there with his eyes fixed on the ground, holding the speaker's staff stiff and still, moving it neither forward nor back, like a man who had never spoken in public — you would have taken him for some sullen fool. But once he let the great voice out of his chest, and the words came driving down like winter snow, then no living man could stand against Odysseus; and we no longer marveled at the look of him."
Then Priam saw Ajax and asked a third time: "And who is that other Greek, great and tall, head and shoulders above the rest of the Argives?"

Helen answered, the long robe trailing, radiant among women: "That is huge Ajax, the wall of the Greeks. And over on the other side, among the Cretans, stands Idomeneus, like a god, with the captains of Crete gathered around him. Often Menelaus, dear to Ares, welcomed him into our house when he came across from Crete. And I can see all the other Greeks now, the bright-eyed men I could name for you one by one. Only two I cannot find anywhere — Castor, breaker of horses, and Polydeuces, the great boxer — my own brothers, the two my mother bore. Either they never left lovely Lacedaemon, or they sailed here in their ships but will not come out into the fighting, in shame at the disgrace and the dishonor I have brought on them."
So she spoke. But the life-giving earth already held them fast, away in Lacedaemon, in their own dear country.

Meanwhile the heralds were bringing the offerings for the oath through the city — two lambs, and wine, the cheer of the earth, in a goatskin; and Idaeus carried the gleaming mixing-bowl and the golden cups. He came up to the old king and roused him: "Up, son of Laomedon. The leading men of the Trojans and the Greeks are calling for you to come down onto the plain and swear a binding oath. Alexandros and Menelaus are to fight with the long spears for the woman; she and all her wealth go to the winner. The rest of us are to swear a peace, so that we Trojans live on here in the rich land of Troy, and the Greeks sail home to Argos and the green country of Achaea."

The old man shuddered to hear it, but he gave the word to yoke the horses, and his men were quick to obey. Priam mounted and drew back the reins, and Antenor climbed up beside him in the splendid chariot, and they drove the fast horses out through the Scaean gates onto the plain. When they reached the Trojans and the Greeks, they stepped down from the chariot onto the teeming earth and walked out into the open ground between the two armies.

At once Agamemnon, lord of men, rose to meet them, and Odysseus, the man of many turns. The proud heralds brought the offerings together for the oath, mixed wine in the bowl, and poured water over the hands of the kings. Then the son of Atreus drew the knife that always hung beside the great scabbard of his sword and cut some hairs from the heads of the lambs, and the heralds passed them around among the leading men of both sides. And Agamemnon lifted his hands and prayed aloud for them all: "Father Zeus, lord of Ida, greatest and most glorious — and you, Sun, who see all things and hear all things — and you Rivers, and you Earth, and you powers below the ground who punish the dead that swore falsely: be our witnesses, and keep faith with these oaths. If Alexandros kills Menelaus, then let him keep Helen and all her wealth, and we will sail home in our seagoing ships. But if fair-haired Menelaus kills Alexandros, then the Trojans give Helen back and all her wealth, and pay the Greeks a fitting penalty besides, one that men yet unborn will remember. And if, once Paris has fallen, Priam and Priam's sons refuse to pay it, then I will stay and fight on for that payment until I see this war to its end."

With that he drew the pitiless bronze across the lambs' throats and laid them on the ground, gasping out their lives, for the knife had taken their strength. Then they dipped wine from the bowl into the cups, and poured it out, and prayed to the gods who live forever — Trojans and Greeks, each man among them: "Zeus, greatest and most glorious, and all you other deathless gods: whichever side is first to break this oath, let their brains run out on the ground the way this wine runs out — theirs and their children's — and let their wives be carried off by other men." So they prayed. But the son of Cronus would not yet grant it.

Then Priam of the line of Dardanus spoke among them: "Hear me, Trojans and Greeks. I am going back now to windswept Ilios. I cannot bring myself to watch with my own eyes my dear son fight Menelaus. Zeus knows, and the other immortal gods know, which of the two is fated to die." So the godlike old man laid the lambs in his chariot, mounted, and drew back the reins, and Antenor climbed up beside him in the splendid car, and the two of them turned and drove home to Ilios.

Then Hector, Priam's son, and brilliant Odysseus first measured out the ground, and then they took two lots and shook them in a bronze helmet, to see which of the two would throw his spear first. And the armies lifted their hands to the gods and prayed — Trojans and Greeks both: "Father Zeus, lord of Ida, greatest and most glorious: whichever of the two set this trouble between us, let him die and go down into the house of the dead, and let the rest of us hold to our oaths in peace."

Great Hector of the flashing helmet shook the lots, looking away — and Paris' lot leaped out first. Then the armies sat down, each man by his horses where his gleaming gear was laid, and Alexandros, husband of lovely-haired Helen, put on his splendid armor. First the greaves, fitted to his shins with silver clasps at the ankle. Next the breastplate of his brother Lycaon, settled to his own body. Over his shoulders he slung the silver-studded bronze sword, and then the great heavy shield. On his strong head he set the crafted helmet, its horsehair crest nodding above him with menace, and he took up a heavy spear that sat well in his grip. And in the same way Menelaus, dear to Ares, armed himself.

When the two had armed, each among his own people, they strode out into the space between the armies with murder in their eyes, and a kind of awe took hold of everyone watching, Trojans and Greeks alike. They came to a stop close together on the measured ground, shaking their spears, each one raging at the other. Alexandros threw first, and his long spear struck the round shield of the son of Atreus — but it did not break through; the point bent back against the strong shield. Then Menelaus drove up with his own spear, and as he did, he prayed to Father Zeus: "Lord Zeus, let me pay back the man who wronged me first — Alexandros — and beat him down under my hands, so that men still unborn will think twice before doing harm to the host who befriends them."

He balanced the long spear and let it fly, and struck the round shield of Alexandros. Straight through the bright shield the heavy spear drove, and on through the worked breastplate, and tore the shirt along his flank — but Alexandros swerved aside, and dodged the black end of death. Then the son of Atreus drew his silver-studded sword, reared back, and brought it down on the ridge of Paris' helmet — and the sword shattered against it, three and four pieces, and fell from his hand. Menelaus groaned and looked up at the wide sky: "Father Zeus — no god is crueler than you. I was sure I had paid Alexandros back for his wrong, and now the sword breaks in my hand, and the spear has flown from my grip for nothing, and I have not killed him."

And with that he sprang at Alexandros, seized him by the horsehair crest of his helmet, spun him around, and started hauling him toward the Greeks — and the embroidered strap, drawn tight under the soft of his throat, was choking him. Menelaus would have dragged him off and won unending glory, but Aphrodite, daughter of Zeus, was watching, and she was quick: she snapped the strap of slaughtered ox-hide, and the empty helmet came away in Menelaus' fist. He swung it around his head and sent it flying to his comrades among the Greeks, who gathered it up. Then he charged in again, hungry to run Paris through with the bronze — but Aphrodite snatched him away, easily, the way a god does, and hid him in a thick mist, and set him down in his own fragrant, vaulted bedchamber.

Then she went herself to call Helen. She found her up on the high tower, the Trojan women thick around her, and she took the shape of an old woman, a wool-carder who had once worked the lovely wool for Helen back in Lacedaemon, and whom Helen loved. In that disguise the goddess plucked at Helen's sweet-scented robe and said: "Come — Alexandros is calling you home. He's there in the bedroom, on the carved bed, glowing with beauty in his fine clothes. You'd never think he had just come from fighting a man — more like he was on his way to a dance, or had just sat down from one."

So she spoke, and stirred Helen's heart in her breast. But when Helen saw the goddess's lovely throat, and her breasts that wake desire, and her glittering eyes, she was struck with wonder, and then with anger, and she said: "You strange, uncanny power — why this longing to deceive me again? Where will you carry me off to next, to some city farther still, somewhere in Phrygia or in lovely Maeonia, if there's another mortal man down there you favor? Is it because Menelaus has beaten Alexandros now, and means to take his hated wife back home — is that why you've come here to me with your treachery? Go sit beside Alexandros yourself, then. Step off the gods' high road. Never set foot on Olympus again. Fret over him, guard him, until he makes you his wife — or makes you his slave. I will not go to him. It would be shameful. I will not warm that man's bed again. Every woman in Troy would have it to throw at me — and I have grief enough in my heart already."

Aphrodite, who loves laughter, rounded on her in fury: "Don't push me, you reckless girl — or I'll let you go, in anger, and hate you as fiercely as I have loved you. I'll set a vicious hatred between the Trojans and the Greeks, and you — you'll come to a wretched end."
So she spoke, and Helen, child of Zeus, was afraid. She drew the white shining veil close about her and went in silence, slipping past the Trojan women unseen, with the goddess leading the way.

When they came to the beautiful house of Alexandros, the serving women turned at once to their work, and Helen, radiant among women, climbed to the high bedchamber. There Aphrodite, who loves laughter, took up a chair with her own hands and carried it over and set it down facing Alexandros. And Helen, daughter of Zeus who bears the storm-shield, sat — but she turned her eyes away from him, and her words came down on her husband hard: "So. Back from the fighting. I wish you had died out there, beaten by the strong man who used to be my husband. You were always boasting how you were the better man, your hands and your spear stronger than Menelaus. Go on, then — challenge him again, fight Menelaus face to face. No — don't. I tell you, stay where you are; don't be fool enough to trade blows with fair-haired Menelaus, or his spear will have you down in a moment."

And Paris answered her: "Don't cut at my heart with these hard words, wife. This time Menelaus won, with Athena's help — but next time it will be me; I have gods on my side as well. Now come, let's lie down together and take our pleasure. Never has desire so wrapped itself around my heart — not even that first day I carried you off from lovely Lacedaemon, sailing away in the seagoing ships, and held you on the island of Cranae, and lay with you in love. Not even then did I want you the way I want you now, with this sweet ache running through me." And he led the way to the bed, and his wife went with him.

So the two of them lay together on the carved bed. But the son of Atreus stalked up and down through the crowd like a wild beast, searching everywhere for Alexandros. And no one — not one of the Trojans, not one of their famous allies — could point him out to Menelaus. They would not have hidden him out of love, if any of them had seen him: they hated him, every one, the way they hated black death. Then Agamemnon, lord of men, spoke out among them: "Hear me, Trojans, and Dardanians, and allies. The victory plainly belongs to Menelaus, dear to Ares. So give Helen back, and all the wealth with her, and pay the penalty besides — a fitting one, that men still to be born will remember."
So spoke the son of Atreus, and all the Greeks roared their approval.

Now the gods sat with Zeus in council on the golden floor of heaven, and Hebe went among them pouring out nectar, and they pledged one another from their golden cups and looked down on the city of Troy. And the son of Cronus set out to needle Hera, talking past her to provoke her: "Menelaus has two goddesses to back him — Hera of Argos and Athena of Alalcomenae — but the two of them only sit here and watch the show, while laughter-loving Aphrodite never leaves Paris's side and turns aside every danger from him. Look — she has just saved him when he thought he was a dead man. And yet the victory belongs to Menelaus. So we have to decide what to do. Shall we set them at each other's throats again, or make peace between the two sides? If you'd all agree to that last, the city of Priam could go on standing, and Menelaus could take Helen home."

So he spoke, and Athena and Hera muttered under their breath, sitting close together, plotting trouble for the Trojans. Athena said nothing — she scowled at her father, a wild fury working in her — but Hera could not hold it in. "Dread son of Cronus," she said, "what kind of talk is that? How can you want to make all my work come to nothing — the sweat I sweated, the horses I wore out, mustering the army against Priam and his sons? Do as you please. But the rest of us gods will not all of us approve."

Deeply angered, Zeus who gathers the clouds answered: "You strange, impossible woman — what have Priam and Priam's sons ever done to you, that you rage on and on to sack the well-built city of Troy? Would nothing satisfy you but to break through the gates and the great walls and eat Priam raw, and his sons, and all the Trojans besides? Then have it your way. Only don't let this quarrel grow into a lasting bitterness between us. And mark what I tell you now, and take it to heart: when the day comes that I want to destroy a city — and it will be one of yours, full of men you love — don't try to hold back my anger. Let me have my way, as I am letting you have yours, against my own will. For of all the cities men live in under the sun and the starry sky, none has stood dearer to my heart than holy Troy, and Priam, and the people of Priam who fight with the good ash spear. My altar there never went without its fair share of the feast, the wine poured out and the savor of burning fat — the honors that are our due."

Ox-eyed lady Hera answered him: "There are three cities I love best of all — Argos, and Sparta, and Mycenae of the wide streets. Raze them whenever they come to anger you. I will not stand in front of them; I will not grudge it. And even if I did grudge it, and tried to stop you, I would gain nothing, since you are far the stronger. But you must not let my labor go for nothing. I too am a god, and I come from the same stock as you: crooked-minded Cronus fathered me, his eldest daughter, and I am honored twice over — by my birth, and because I am called your wife, and you rule over all the immortals. So let us give way to each other in this, you to me and I to you, and the rest of the gods will follow our lead. Now order Athena down to the fighting at once, and let her work it so that the Trojans are the first to break their sworn oath and strike at the proud Greeks."

The father of gods and men did not refuse her. At once he spoke winged words to Athena: "Go quickly, down into the armies, among the Trojans and the Greeks, and work it so that the Trojans are the first to break their oath and strike at the proud Greeks."

It was the very thing Athena was burning to do, and down she shot from the peaks of Olympus. She came like a star that the son of crooked-minded Cronus sends as a sign to sailors, or to some great army of men, a blazing thing that throws off sparks as it goes — and in that shape Athena flashed to earth, dropping between the two armies. Awe took the men who saw it, Trojans and bronze-clad Greeks alike, and a man would turn to the one beside him and say: "This means hard war and the din of battle again — or else Zeus, who holds the keys of war and peace for men, is about to make peace between the two sides."

So the men were saying to one another. Then Athena went into the Trojan ranks in the likeness of Laodocus, son of Antenor, a strong spearman, hunting for godlike Pandarus. She found him standing among the stout ranks of shield-bearers who had followed him from the banks of the Aesepus. She came up close and spoke winged words: "Will you do as I say, brave son of Lycaon? Then you would dare to send a fast arrow at Menelaus — and win the thanks and the glory of all the Trojans, and most of all of prince Paris. He, before any of them, would load you with shining gifts, if he saw Menelaus, the warlike son of Atreus, laid out on the funeral pyre, brought down by an arrow from your hand. Come — let fly at Menelaus, and make a vow to Apollo, the wolf-god, the lord of the bow, that you will offer him a fine hecatomb of firstling lambs when you come home to your holy city of Zeleia."

So Athena spoke, and won over the fool's heart in him. At once he uncovered his polished bow — made from the horns of a wild ibex he had shot one day as it sprang from a rock; he had been lying in wait, and the arrow caught it under the breast and it dropped backward off the cliff. Its horns had grown sixteen palms long, and a craftsman in horn had worked them, fitted them together, smoothed them down, and capped them with gold. Pandarus bent the bow and braced it carefully against the ground, and his brave men held their shields up in front of him, so the warlike Greeks would not rush him before he had hit Menelaus. He lifted the lid of his quiver and took out an arrow, never shot, fledged with the agonies of death. Quickly he set the bitter shaft to the string and made his vow to Apollo, the wolf-god, the lord of the bow — that he would offer a fine hecatomb of firstling lambs when he came home to his holy city of Zeleia. He notched the arrow and drew the ox-gut string back to his chest, the iron point to the bow; and when he had bent the great bow into a circle, it sang, and the string cried out, and the sharp arrow leapt away, hungry to fly through the crowd.

But the blessed, undying gods did not forget you then, Menelaus. First of all, the daughter of Zeus who drives the spoils of war stood in front of you and turned the piercing arrow aside. She brushed it from your skin the way a mother brushes a fly from her child while he lies in sweet sleep, and she steered it down to where the golden clasps of your belt held it tight, where the corselet was doubled over on itself. The bitter arrow struck the fitted belt and drove straight through it, and on through the finely worked corselet, and through the guard of mail he wore underneath next to his skin to keep off spears and arrows — the thing that saved him most of all, and yet the arrow tore through even that, and grazed the surface of the skin, and at once the dark blood came running from the wound.

As when a woman of Maeonia or Caria stains ivory with crimson dye, to make a cheek-piece for a horse's bridle — it lies stored in a treasure-room, and many a horseman longs to carry it, but it is kept aside as a king's treasure, a glory to the horse and a pride to the man who drives him — so, Menelaus, your shapely thighs were stained with blood, and your legs, and your fine ankles below.

When Agamemnon, lord of men, saw the dark blood running from the wound, a shudder went through him; and warlike Menelaus shuddered too — until he saw that the barbs of the point and the binding-thread still stood clear of the flesh, and then the heart came back into his chest. But Agamemnon, holding his brother by the hand, groaned from the depths of him, and the men around them groaned along with him. "Dear brother," he said, "so it was your death I sealed when I swore that truce — when I sent you out alone, in front of the Greeks, to fight for us. The Trojans have trampled the oath; they have shot you down. But the oath is not dead — not the blood of the lambs, not the unmixed wine we poured, not the right hands we clasped and trusted in. If the Olympian does not bring it home now, he will bring it home later, and they will pay in full — with their own lives, with their wives, with their children. For this I know in my heart and my mind: the day is coming when holy Troy will fall, and Priam, and all the people of Priam who fight with the good ash spear; when the son of Cronus, throned high in the bright air, will shake his dark storm-shield over the whole city in his anger at this treachery. All this will come to pass. But the grief will be mine, Menelaus, beyond bearing, if you die now and fill out the measure of your life. I would go back to thirsty Argos in disgrace — for the Greeks will turn their minds at once to the land of their fathers. We would leave Argive Helen for Priam and the Trojans to gloat over, and your bones would rot in the ground here at Troy, your work undone. And some swaggering Trojan would jump on the grave of glorious Menelaus and say: 'May Agamemnon's anger always end like this — the way he brought his Greek army here for nothing, and now has sailed home to his own country with empty ships, and left brave Menelaus behind.' That is what one of them will say. On that day, let the wide earth open and swallow me."

But fair-haired Menelaus reassured him: "Take heart, and don't frighten the men. The point hasn't fixed in a fatal spot. The bright belt turned it first, and under that the kilt of mail and the guard the bronze-smiths beat out for me."
And Agamemnon, lord of men, answered: "I pray it's so, dear Menelaus. But let a healer look at the wound and lay drugs on it to ease the dark pain."

He turned to the herald Talthybius: "Talthybius — go, quick as you can, and call Machaon, the son of Asclepius the great healer, to come and see warlike Menelaus. Some Trojan or Lycian, a man skilled with the bow, has shot him — a glory for the archer, a grief for us."

The herald heard and obeyed. He went through the ranks of the bronze-clad Greeks, searching for the warrior Machaon, and found him standing among the strong lines of shield-men who had followed him from Tricca, where they pasture horses. He came up beside him and spoke winged words: "On your feet, son of Asclepius — Agamemnon, lord of men, is calling for you, to come and see warlike Menelaus. Some Trojan or Lycian, a man skilled with the bow, has shot him — a glory for the archer, a grief for us."

So he spoke, and stirred the heart in Machaon's chest. They went back through the wide army of the Greeks, and came to where fair-haired Menelaus had been hit, and the captains were gathered in a ring around him. Machaon stepped into the middle of them, and at once drew the arrow out of the fitted belt; and as he pulled, the sharp barbs bent back. He undid the bright belt, and under it the kilt of mail and the guard the bronze-smiths had made; and when he had found the wound where the bitter arrow had struck, he sucked the blood from it and spread on it, with sure skill, the soothing drugs that Chiron had once given his father out of friendship.
While they were busy over Menelaus, who roars in battle, the lines of the Trojans, shields up, came on against them, and the Greeks took up their armor again, with a will for war.

And now you would not have seen Agamemnon dozing, or hanging back, or shy of the fight — no, he was straining for the battle where men win glory. He left his horses and his chariot bright with bronze, and his man Eurymedon, son of Ptolemaeus, son of Peiraeus, held the snorting team off to one side, with orders to keep them close at hand for whenever his legs grew weary of ranging up and down and giving commands; for he went among the lines on foot. Wherever he saw the men keen and quick, he stood beside them and spurred them on: "Greeks — don't slacken your fury for a moment. Father Zeus will be no friend to liars. The men who were first to break the oath and strike us — the vultures will eat their soft flesh, and we'll carry off their dear wives and their little children in our ships, on the day we take their city."

But wherever he saw men shrinking from the hateful war, he tore into them in anger: "You Greeks — you boasters, you disgraces — have you no shame? Why do you stand here stunned, like fawns that run themselves out across a wide plain and then stop, helpless, with no fight left in them? That's how you stand here, dazed, with no will to fight. Are you waiting for the Trojans to reach the sterns of our fine ships, drawn up there on the gray shore — waiting to see whether the son of Cronus will stretch his hand over you and save you?"

So he ranged through the ranks, taking command. He came through the press to the Cretans, arming around fiery Idomeneus, who stood at their head, brave as a wild boar, while Meriones was driving up the rear companies. Agamemnon, lord of men, was glad to see them, and spoke warmly to Idomeneus: "Idomeneus — I honor you above all the fast-horsed Greeks, in war and in everything else, and at the table too. When the other captains mix the bright wine and each is given his measured share, your cup stands full like my own, to drink whenever your heart moves you. So now — into the fight, and show yourself the man you have always been proud to be."

Idomeneus, lord of the Cretans, answered: "Son of Atreus — I will be the trusty friend I promised to be from the first. Go now, rouse the rest of the long-haired Greeks, and let us join battle at once, since the Trojans have trampled their oath. Death and ruin are theirs in the days to come, for being the first to break faith and strike us."

So he spoke, and the son of Atreus passed on, glad at heart. He came through the crowd to the two named Ajax, arming themselves with a thick mass of foot-soldiers around them. As when a goatherd from a lookout above the sea watches a storm come on across the deep before the West Wind — out on the water it stands black as pitch and bears down on him, a great whirlwind, and he is afraid and drives his flock into a cave — so under the two Ajaxes the close ranks of the strong young men moved into battle, a dark mass bristling with shields and spears. Agamemnon, lord of men, was glad to see them, and his words flew out: "You two — captains of the bronze-clad Greeks — I'll give you no orders; that would be wrong, for of your own selves you drive your men to fight with all their strength. Father Zeus, Athena, Apollo — if only every man in the army had a heart like yours! Then the city of lord Priam would soon bow under our hands, taken and sacked."

With that he left them and went on to Nestor, the clear speaker of Pylos, who was marshaling his men and urging them to the fight — and around him were Pelagon and Alastor, Chromius, Haemon, and Bias, shepherd of the people. He set the horsemen with their chariots and teams in the front rank, and behind them the foot-soldiers, brave men and many, the wall of the war; and the cowards he drove into the middle, so that a man would have to fight whether he wanted to or not. He gave his orders to the horsemen first, telling them to hold their teams hard in hand and not let the lines fall into confusion: "Let no man, trusting his horsemanship or his strength, charge out ahead of the rest to take on the Trojans alone — and let no man fall back; that only weakens us. When a man comes within reach of an enemy chariot from his own, let him stab with his spear — that is far the best way. This is how the men of old took walls and cities: this resolve, this spirit was in their chests."

So the old man urged them on, schooled in war from long ago, and Agamemnon, lord of men, was glad to see it. His words flew out to him: "Old man — I wish the strength in your limbs matched the spirit in your chest, and your body were as sure as your judgment. But age, the common burden of all men, has come down on you. I wish it had fallen on some other man, and that you were still young."

And Nestor, the horseman of Gerene, answered: "Son of Atreus — I too would gladly be the man I was the day I cut down great Ereuthalion. But the gods do not give a man everything at once. I was young then; now old age is on me. Even so, I'll go among the horsemen and guide them with counsel and with words — for that is the privilege left to the old. The young men will throw the spears, the men who came after me, who can still trust their strength."

So he spoke, and the son of Atreus passed on, glad at heart. He found Menestheus, son of Peteos, the driver of horses, standing idle, and around him the Athenians, who raise the war cry in battle. And nearby stood resourceful Odysseus, with the ranks of his strong Cephallenians around him. They were standing still, for the war cry had not yet reached them — the lines of Trojans and Greeks had only just begun to stir — and so they waited, watching for some other Greek column to go forward against the Trojans and open the fight. When Agamemnon, lord of men, saw this, he rounded on them: "Son of Peteos, king bred up by Zeus — and you, master of evil cunning, your mind set on your own gain — why do the two of you hang back, cowering, waiting on the rest? It would suit you two to stand among the very first and meet the scorching fight. You're the first to hear when I call you to the feast, when we elders of the Greeks lay out a banquet. Glad enough then to eat your fill of roast meat and drink the honeyed wine as long as you please. But now you'd be glad to watch ten Greek columns go in ahead of you with the pitiless bronze."

Resourceful Odysseus glared at him and answered: "Son of Atreus — what kind of word has got past your teeth? How can you say I hold back from the fight, when we Greeks wake the keen edge of war against the Trojans? You'll see — if you care to, and if it's any concern of yours — the dear father of Telemachus closing with the front ranks of the horse-taming Trojans. This is empty talk you're making."

When Agamemnon, lord of men, saw that he was angry, he smiled, and took his words back: "Royal son of Laertes, resourceful Odysseus — I have no blame to lay on you, no orders to give you. I know the heart in your chest is set on what is right; you and I are of one mind. Come, we'll make this good later. And if any harsh thing has been said now, may the gods scatter it to the winds."

With that he left them and went on to others. He found the son of Tydeus, proud Diomedes, standing by his horses and his bolted chariot, with Sthenelus, son of Capaneus, beside him; and he tore into him too: "Son of Tydeus — tamer of horses — why do you stand here cowering, peering down the lanes of the battle? It was not Tydeus's way to shrink like this. He fought far out ahead of his men, against the enemy — so they say who saw him at his work, for I never met him or set eyes on him myself; but they say there was no man like him. Once he came to Mycenae, not as an enemy but as a guest, with godlike Polynices, raising an army; they were marching on the holy walls of Thebes, and they begged us hard to give them picked men to help. Our people were willing to grant it, but Zeus turned them against it with signs of ill omen. So Tydeus and Polynices went on their way. They came as far as the deep-grassed, rush-grown banks of the Asopus, and there the Greeks sent Tydeus ahead as their envoy. On he went, and found a great crowd of the sons of Cadmus feasting in the house of mighty Eteocles. Stranger though he was, the horseman Tydeus felt no fear, alone among so many: he challenged them all to contests, and won every one, easily — Athena was that great a help to him. The horse-driving Cadmeans were stung, and on his way back they set an ambush for him, fifty young men under two captains — godlike Maeon, son of Haemon, and Polyphontes, son of Autophonus, steady in battle. But Tydeus brought a foul death down on all of them; he killed every man but one — Maeon, whom he sent home in obedience to the gods' signs. That was Tydeus of Aetolia. But the son he fathered is a worse man in battle, and a better one only at talk."

So he spoke. Strong Diomedes said nothing — he took the king's rebuke and held his peace, in awe of him. But the son of glorious Capaneus answered back: "Son of Atreus — don't tell lies, when you know how to speak the truth. We claim to be far better men than our fathers were. We took seven-gated Thebes, the two of us, leading a smaller force against a stronger wall, trusting the gods' signs and the help of Zeus — while they died through their own blind folly. So never set our fathers in the same honor as us."

Strong Diomedes turned a hard look on him: "Hold your tongue, friend, and listen to me. I don't blame Agamemnon, shepherd of the people, for driving the Greeks on to fight. The glory will follow him if we Greeks cut the Trojans down and take holy Troy — and the great grief will be his too, if the Greeks are beaten. So come — let us turn our minds to our own fighting fury."
He spoke, and sprang to the ground from his chariot in his armor, and the bronze rang terribly on the body of the rushing king — a sound to put fear into the bravest heart.

As when, on a thundering shore, wave after wave of the sea comes driving in before the West Wind — far out on the deep it lifts its crest first, then breaks roaring on the dry land, and arches high over the headlands and spits the salt foam into the air — so, wave on wave, the close ranks of the Greeks moved without stopping into battle. Each captain called the orders to his own; the rest came on in silence — you would not have thought so vast a host had a voice in it at all, so quietly they went, in dread of their commanders. The worked armor blazed on them as they marched in their lines. But the Trojans — like the countless ewes of a rich man, standing penned to be milked, bleating without end at the sound of their lambs — so the cry of the Trojans went up across the wide army, no single shout, no one speech; their tongues were mixed, men called from many lands. These Ares drove on; the Greeks were driven by gray-eyed Athena — and with them went Terror, and Rout, and Strife, who rages on and never tires, the sister and companion of man-killing Ares: Strife, who rears up small at first, then plants her head in the sky while her feet still walk the earth. She it was who went among them now, casting her hatred into the thick of them, the cause of men's groaning, and made the bitterness grow on every side.

And when they had come together into one ground, shield clashed against shield, spear against spear, the fury of men in their bronze armor; the bossed shields rammed one another, and a great roar went up. There were screams of the dying and shouts of the men who killed them, and the earth ran with blood. As when two rivers in winter spate come down the mountains and hurl their racing waters together into one ravine, out of their great springs, deep in a gorge — and far off on the hills the shepherd hears the thunder of it — so was the shouting and the toil as the two armies met.

Antilochus was the first to bring down a Trojan in his armor, a brave man in the front line, Echepolus, son of Thalysius. He struck him first on the ridge of his crested helmet, and the bronze point drove into his forehead and through the bone, and the dark closed over his eyes, and he toppled like a falling tower in the hard fighting. As he dropped, lord Elephenor, son of Chalcodon, captain of the great-hearted Abantes, caught him by the feet and began dragging him out from under the flying spears, in a rush to strip his armor — but his rush was short-lived. Great-hearted Agenor saw him hauling the body away, and as Elephenor bent over it his flank was left bare beside his shield, and Agenor drove the bronze-shod spear into it and brought him down. So he died, and over his body the deadly work of Trojans and Greeks flared up, and they leapt at one another like wolves, man grappling man.

Then Ajax, son of Telamon, struck down the son of Anthemion, a fine young man in his bloom, Simoeisius — whom his mother had borne by the banks of the Simois, coming down from Ida where she had gone with her parents to look at the flocks; and so they named him Simoeisius. But he never paid his dear parents back for raising him; his life was cut short under the spear of great-hearted Ajax. As he came on among the front-rankers, Ajax struck him in the chest beside the right nipple, and the bronze spear drove straight through his shoulder, and he fell in the dust like a poplar — a smooth-trunked tree grown tall in the wet ground of a great water-meadow, with branches springing only at the crown. A wheelwright fells it with his bright iron to bend a wheel-rim for a fine chariot, and it lies seasoning by the riverbank. So Simoeisius, son of Anthemion, lay where godlike Ajax had felled him. Then Antiphus of the gleaming corselet, a son of Priam, hurled his sharp spear at Ajax through the crowd — and missed him, but struck Leucus, Odysseus's brave comrade, in the groin as he was dragging Simoeisius's body to the other side. Leucus fell across it and let it slip from his hands. Odysseus's heart blazed at his death, and he strode out through the front ranks in his shining bronze and came up close, and stood and threw his bright spear, looking carefully about him — and the Trojans gave ground before the throw. The spear did not fly for nothing: it struck Democoon, a bastard son of Priam, who had come to him from Abydos, from his post over the swift mares. Odysseus, raging for his dead friend, struck him with the spear on one temple, and the bronze point came out through the other; the dark closed over his eyes, and he fell with a crash, and his armor clattered on him. Then the front-line Trojans gave way, glorious Hector with them; and the Greeks raised a great shout, and dragged off the dead, and pushed on, further forward. But Apollo looked down from Pergamus and was angry, and he called to the Trojans: "Up, you horse-taming Trojans! Don't give in to the Greeks. Their skin is not stone, and it is not iron, to turn the cutting bronze when you strike them. And remember — Achilles, the son of lovely-haired Thetis, is not fighting. He sits by the ships, nursing his anger."

So the dread god cried to them from the high city. And on the other side the daughter of Zeus, glorious Athena, ranged through the army of the Greeks, urging them on wherever she saw them giving ground.

Then doom closed over Diores, son of Amarynceus. A jagged stone struck him by the ankle of his right leg, hurled by the captain of the Thracians, Peirous, son of Imbrasus, who had come from Aenus. The pitiless stone crushed both the bone and the two tendons utterly, and he went down on his back in the dust, stretching out both hands to his companions, gasping out his life. And Peirous, the man who had hit him, ran in and stabbed him with the spear beside the navel, and his bowels spilled to the ground, and the dark closed over his eyes. But as Peirous sprang back, Thoas of Aetolia caught him with a spear in the chest above the nipple, and the bronze fixed in his lung. Thoas came up close, wrenched the heavy spear out of his chest, and drew his sharp sword and drove it into the middle of his belly and took his life — but he could not strip the armor, for the Thracians stood thick around the body, men who wear their hair in a topknot, holding their long spears out, and for all his size and his courage and his force they shoved him back, and he gave ground. So the two lay stretched in the dust beside each other, the captain of the Thracians and the captain of the bronze-clad Epeans, and around them many more were cut down.

And now no man could have come into that fight and made light of it — not even one who walked through the middle of it untouched, unwounded, with Pallas Athena leading him by the hand and warding off the storm of flying weapons. For that day many Trojans and many Greeks lay side by side, face-down in the dust.

Now Pallas Athena filled Diomedes, son of Tydeus, with courage and fire, so that he would stand out among all the Greeks and win himself glory. She made a flame stream from his shield and helmet, steady and unwearying, like the star that burns brightest of all in late summer when it has bathed in the streams of Ocean. Such a fire she kindled on his head and his shoulders, and she drove him into the thick of the fighting, where the press was densest.

There was a Trojan named Dares, a rich and honored man, priest of Hephaestus, and he had two sons, Phegeus and Idaeus, both skilled in every kind of fighting. These two broke from the ranks and came at Diomedes together, riding in their chariot while he stood on foot. When they were close, Phegeus let his spear fly first — but it passed over Diomedes' left shoulder and missed. Then Diomedes threw, and his bronze did not fly for nothing: it struck Phegeus full in the chest, by the nipple, and knocked him from the car. Idaeus did not dare to stand over his dead brother's body; he leaped from the chariot and ran, or he too would have died there. But Hephaestus saved him, wrapping him in darkness so the old priest would not be utterly crushed with grief. And the son of Tydeus drove off the horses and gave them to his men to take back to the ships.

When the Trojans saw the two sons of Dares — one in flight, the other dead beside his chariot — their hearts shook. Then Athena took Ares by the hand and said: "Ares, Ares — butcher of men, blood-soaked stormer of walls — why don't we leave the Trojans and the Greeks to fight it out alone, and let Zeus hand the victory to whichever side he pleases? Let's stand aside, and keep clear of his anger." With that she led raging Ares out of the battle and sat him down on the high banks of the Scamander.

Now the Greeks drove the Trojans back, and every leader among them killed his man. First Agamemnon, lord of men, hurled mighty Odius, the captain of the Halizones, out of his chariot: as he turned to run, the spear struck him square between the shoulders and drove on through his chest, and he fell with a crash, his armor clanging around him.

Then Idomeneus killed Phaestus, son of Borus the Maeonian, who had come from Tarne. As Phaestus was climbing into his chariot, Idomeneus' long spear caught him in the right shoulder, and the darkness of death closed over him as he toppled from the car; and Idomeneus' men stripped the armor from his body.

Menelaus, son of Atreus, killed Scamandrius, son of Strophius, a fine huntsman — Artemis herself had taught him to bring down every wild thing that the mountain forests breed. But the goddess of the chase could not save him now, nor could his own famed skill with the bow: Menelaus' spear took him in the back as he ran, struck him between the shoulders, and drove on through his chest, and he pitched forward, his armor ringing around him.

Meriones killed Phereclus, son of Tecton, son of Harmon, a man whose hands knew every kind of clever craft, for Pallas Athena had loved him dearly. It was Phereclus who had built the ships for Paris — the ships that began all the trouble, that brought ruin on the Trojans and on Paris himself; for he had not understood what the gods had decreed. Meriones ran him down as he fled and struck him in the right buttock; the point drove through the bone into the bladder, and he went down on his knees, screaming, and death took him.

Meges killed Pedaeus, son of Antenor. He was a bastard, but Theano had raised him as one of her own children, out of love for her husband. The son of Phyleus closed on him and drove a spear into the back of his neck; it cut on through, under his tongue and among his teeth, and he bit the cold bronze and fell dead in the dust.

And Eurypylus, son of Euaemon, killed Hypsenor, son of proud Dolopion — a man who had been made priest of the river Scamander and was honored by his people like a god. Eurypylus chased him as he fled, swung his sword, and lopped off his strong arm at the shoulder. The bloody hand dropped to the ground, and red death and overpowering fate closed his eyes.

So they labored on in the hard fighting. But you could not have told which side the son of Tydeus was on — whether he ran with the Trojans or the Greeks — for he swept across the plain like a winter river in flood, a torrent that has burst its banks and tears down the dikes in its rush. No piled-up embankment holds it, no wall of a fruitful vineyard, when it comes on suddenly, swollen with the rain of Zeus, and lays waste the work of many strong men in a moment. So before Diomedes the close ranks of the Trojans were scattered and broken, and for all their numbers they could not stand against him.

But the son of Lycaon — Pandarus — saw him storming over the plain, driving whole ranks before him. He bent his bow and shot, and struck him on the right shoulder, on the plate of his cuirass; the arrow tore straight through, and the blood ran down over the bronze. Pandarus shouted in triumph: "On, Trojans, spur your horses on! The best of the Greeks is hit — and he won't last long under that wound, if it was truly lord Apollo who sped me here from Lycia!"

So he boasted; but the arrow had not killed Diomedes. He pulled back to his chariot and his horses, to Sthenelus, son of Capaneus, and said: "Up, dear son of Capaneus — get down and draw this arrow out of my shoulder." Sthenelus jumped from the car and pulled the shaft clear, and the blood came spurting out through the rings of his shirt. Then Diomedes prayed: "Hear me, child of Zeus who holds the storm-shield, tireless one. If ever you stood by my father in the thick of battle and loved him, stand by me now. Bring this man within a spear's throw — let me kill the one who shot me before I could see him, and now boasts I won't look much longer on the light of the sun."

So he prayed, and Pallas Athena heard him. She made his limbs light, his feet and his hands quick, and she came close and spoke: "Take heart, Diomedes — go and fight the Trojans. I've put your father's spirit in your chest, the fearless drive of Tydeus the horseman. And I've taken the mist from your eyes that was on them before, so you can tell a god from a man. If any other god comes here to test you, do not fight him — but if Aphrodite, daughter of Zeus, comes into the battle, her you may wound. Drive your bronze into her."

With that the bright-eyed goddess was gone, and the son of Tydeus went back into the front ranks. He had been hot to fight the Trojans before; now he burned with three times the fury, like a lion that a shepherd has wounded but not killed as it sprang into the sheepfold — he has only stung it to rage. The shepherd cannot fight it off; he hides among the buildings, and the abandoned sheep panic and pile on one another, while the lion leaps back out over the high wall. So Diomedes, raging, fell on the Trojans.

He killed Astynous and Hypeiron, shepherd of his people — one he struck above the nipple with the spear, the other he hacked with the sword at the collarbone, shearing the shoulder clean from neck and back. He left them and went after Abas and Polyidus, sons of old Eurydamas, the reader of dreams; but the old man read no dreams for them when they did not come home, for mighty Diomedes made an end of them both. Then he chased down Xanthus and Thoon, the two late-born sons of Phaenops — sons of his old age, with no other to inherit. Diomedes took both their lives and left their father nothing but grief and tears, for he never welcomed them home alive, and strangers divided his wealth.

Then he came on two sons of Priam in a single chariot, Echemmon and Chromius. As a lion springs on a cow or a heifer grazing in the brush and breaks its neck, so Diomedes threw them both from the car for all their struggling, stripped their armor, and gave the horses to his men to drive back to the ships.

Now Aeneas saw him cutting whole ranks to pieces, and he went through the storm of spears looking for Pandarus. When he found the brave son of Lycaon he said: "Pandarus — where is your bow now, and your feathered arrows, and the fame that no man here can match, and no man in Lycia either? Lift your hands to Zeus and let an arrow fly at this man who's lording it over the field and has done us so much harm — unless he's some god, angry with the Trojans over a sacrifice, and gods are hard to fight."

And the son of Lycaon answered: "Aeneas, counselor of the bronze-clad Trojans, he looks to me like the son of Tydeus — I know him by his shield, by the visor of his helmet, by his horses. But I can't be sure he isn't a god. If he is the man I think, he's not raging like this without some god beside him, hidden in cloud, who turned my arrow when it had already hit him. For I shot him — struck him square on the right shoulder, clean through the plate of his cuirass — and I was sure I'd sent him down to Hades, and still I haven't killed him. Some god is angry with me. And I have no chariot, no horses here — eleven fine new cars stand in my father Lycaon's halls, fresh from the builder, cloths spread over them, a team of horses by each, champing white barley. Again and again the old man told me, when I left, to bring chariots and lead the Trojans from horseback. I wouldn't listen — I was sparing the horses, afraid they'd go hungry in a great siege, used as they were to eating their fill — and so I came on foot to Ilios, trusting in my bow. And the bow has failed me. I've hit two of their champions now, the son of Atreus and the son of Tydeus, and drawn real blood from both — and only made them fiercer. It was an evil day I took this bow from its peg to lead my men to Troy for Hector's sake. If I ever get home and lay eyes on my country and my wife and my great house again, let some stranger cut my head off if I don't snap this bow with my own hands and throw it on the fire — for all the good it's done me, it might as well be wind."

Aeneas answered: "Talk no more like that. Nothing will change until the two of us go against this man with chariot and horses and test him with our weapons. Get up beside me — see how the horses of Tros can run, how they can chase and wheel and flee across the plain. They'll carry us safe back to the city if Zeus hands the glory to Diomedes again. Take the whip and the reins, and I'll dismount to fight — or you face him, and I'll handle the horses."

"Aeneas," said the son of Lycaon, "keep the reins yourself and drive. The horses will pull better under the hand they know, if we have to run from the son of Tydeus. If they miss the sound of your voice, they may bolt and refuse to carry us out, and Diomedes will be on us and kill us both and take the team. So drive your own horses, and I'll meet the man with my spear."

They mounted the gleaming chariot and drove the fast horses straight at the son of Tydeus. Sthenelus saw them coming and called out: "Diomedes, dearest to my heart — I see two strong men bearing down on you, men of great might. One is the archer Pandarus, son of Lycaon; the other is Aeneas, whose father is great-hearted Anchises and whose mother is Aphrodite. Mount, and let us pull back. Don't go raging on like this in the front — you'll get yourself killed."

But Diomedes scowled at him: "Don't talk to me of running — you won't talk me into it. It's not in my blood to fight from behind or cower; my strength is still in me. I won't even climb into the car — I'll go at them on foot. Pallas Athena will not let me be afraid. Their horses won't carry both of those men away from us — not even if one of them gets clear. And listen, fix this in your mind: if Athena grants me the glory of killing both, rein in our own horses here, lash the reins to the chariot rail, and then make a rush for the horses of Aeneas and drive them out from the Trojans to the Greeks. They come from the stock that Zeus once gave to Tros, the best horses under the sun and the dawn — King Anchises bred from that line on the sly, putting his mares to them behind Laomedon's back. To take them would be great glory."

While the two of them were talking, the others came on fast, and the son of Lycaon spoke first: "Tough, brave son of noble Tydeus — so my arrow didn't bring you down. Now I'll see what my spear can do." He balanced it and hurled it; it struck Diomedes' shield, and the bronze point drove through and on to the breastplate. Pandarus shouted: "Now you're hit clean through the belly — you won't hold out long, and the glory is mine!" But Diomedes, not shaken at all, answered: "You've missed, not hit. And I don't think the two of you are done with this until one of you, at least, has glutted hard-fighting Ares with his blood."

With that he threw, and Athena guided the spear to Pandarus' nose, beside the eye. It crashed in among his white teeth, and the merciless bronze sheared through the root of his tongue and came out at the base of the chin. He fell from the chariot, his bright armor clashing around him, and the swift horses shied in terror; and there his life and his strength were undone.

Aeneas leaped down with his shield and his long spear, afraid the Greeks would drag the body away. He stood over it like a lion sure of its strength, his spear and his round shield held before him, ready to kill whoever came against him, with a terrible cry. But the son of Tydeus caught up a stone in his hand — a huge thing, a mass that two men could not lift, men such as live now; yet he raised it alone, with ease — and he hurled it and struck Aeneas where the thigh turns in the hip, in the joint men call the cup-bone. The stone crushed the socket and snapped both tendons, and the jagged edge tore the skin away. The hero sank to his knees, propped himself on the ground with one heavy hand, and the dark night came down over his eyes.

And now Aeneas, lord of men, would have died there, had his mother not seen it — Aphrodite, daughter of Zeus, who had borne him to Anchises among the cattle. She threw her white arms around her dear son and drew a fold of her shining robe over him, a shield against the spears, so that no Greek could drive bronze into his chest and take his life. So she carried her son out of the fighting. But the son of Capaneus did not forget the orders Diomedes had given him. He tied his own horses clear of the uproar, lashing the reins to the chariot rail; then he sprang at the horses of Aeneas, drove them from the Trojans to the Greeks, and gave them to Deipylus — the comrade he prized above all the rest, for they were of one mind — to take to the hollow ships. And then he mounted his own car again, gripped the reins, and drove hard after the son of Tydeus.

But Diomedes was already after the Cyprian with his pitiless bronze, for he knew her for a weak goddess, not one of those who rule the battles of men, like Athena or Enyo the sacker of cities. He chased her through the great crowd, and when he caught her at last he lunged and stabbed at the surface of her soft hand. The spear tore through the divine robe that the Graces themselves had woven for her, and pierced the skin at the base of the palm, above the wrist; and out flowed the immortal blood of the goddess — ichor, such as runs in the blessed gods, for they eat no bread and drink no gleaming wine, and so they have no blood as we do, and are called the deathless ones. She shrieked and let her son fall — but Phoebus Apollo caught him up in his arms and hid him in a dark cloud, so that no Greek could drive bronze into his chest and take his life. And Diomedes shouted after her: "Give way, daughter of Zeus — leave war and battle alone. Isn't it enough that you seduce soft women? Come near the fighting again, and I think you'll learn to shudder at the very word."

She fled, beside herself with pain, in agony, her fair skin fouled. Iris, swift as the wind, drew her out of the press and away. She found furious Ares sitting off to the left of the battle, his spear and his fast horses resting on a cloud. Aphrodite dropped to her knees before her brother and begged him for his team: "Dear brother, save me — give me your horses, so I can reach Olympus, where the gods live. I'm in terrible pain. A mortal wounded me, the son of Tydeus, who would fight Father Zeus himself now." So Ares gave her his gold-bridled horses, and she climbed into the car, sick at heart, with Iris beside her. Iris took the reins and lashed them on, and they flew willingly up to high Olympus, the home of the gods. There fleet Iris reined them in, unyoked them, and set ambrosial fodder before them, and Aphrodite threw herself into the lap of her mother, Dione.

Dione folded her daughter in her arms and stroked her, and said: "Which of the gods of heaven has treated you like this, dear child, as if you'd been caught doing some open wrong?" And Aphrodite, who loves laughter, answered through her tears: "It was proud Diomedes, the son of Tydeus, who wounded me — because I was carrying my dear son out of the fighting, Aeneas, whom I love beyond all others. This is no longer a war of Trojans and Greeks; now the Greeks are fighting the gods themselves."

"Bear up, my child," Dione answered, "and endure it, hard as it is. Many of us who live on Olympus have suffered at the hands of men, and we lay heavy griefs on one another too. Ares suffered, when Otus and Ephialtes, the sons of Aloeus, bound him in cruel chains and shut him in a bronze jar for thirteen months — and Ares, insatiable for war, would have died there, had not their stepmother, lovely Eeriboea, told Hermes, who stole him out half-spent. And Hera suffered, when the mighty son of Amphitryon struck her in the right breast with a three-barbed arrow, and the pain would not let go of her. And monstrous Hades suffered, when that same man — the son of Zeus who holds the storm-shield — shot him with a swift arrow at the gates of the dead and gave him over to agony. He went to the house of Zeus on high Olympus, sick with pain, the shaft driven deep in his great shoulder, and the arrow tormented him until Paeon spread soothing herbs on the wound and healed him; for he was not made to die. Reckless man, brute, who did not shrink from his sins, who used his bow to wound the gods who hold Olympus. And now the bright-eyed goddess Athena has set this Diomedes on you — fool that he is, not to know in his heart that a man who fights the gods does not live long, and no child climbs his knees and calls him father when he comes home from war and the dread fighting. So let the son of Tydeus take care, strong as he is, that no one stronger than you comes to fight him — or one day his good wife Aegialeia, daughter of Adrestus, will wake the whole house with her wailing as she mourns the husband of her youth, the best of the Greeks: Diomedes, breaker of horses."

With that Dione wiped the ichor from her daughter's wrist with both her hands; the wound closed, the heavy pain eased. But Athena and Hera, watching, began to needle Zeus with their mockery. Athena spoke first: "Father Zeus — will you be angry if I say something? I think the Cyprian must have been coaxing some Greek woman to run off with the Trojans she loves so well, and while she stroked one of those fine-robed Greek ladies she scratched her delicate hand on a golden pin." The father of gods and men smiled, and called golden Aphrodite to him: "Fighting is not your work, my child. See to the lovely business of marriage, and leave all this to swift Ares and to Athena."

So they talked. But Diomedes leaped again at Aeneas, though he knew Apollo himself held his arms around him. He had no fear even of the great god — he was set on killing Aeneas and stripping that famous armor. Three times he charged, hot to cut him down, and three times Apollo struck back his shining shield. But when he came on a fourth time, like something more than a man, Apollo who works from afar cried out at him in a voice of terror: "Think, son of Tydeus, and fall back. Don't try to set yourself level with the gods. The race of immortal gods and the race of men who walk the ground are not the same thing."

So the son of Tydeus gave ground a little, to escape the wrath of Apollo who strikes from afar. And Apollo carried Aeneas out of the crowd and set him down in sacred Pergamus, where his own temple stood; and there, in the great sanctuary, Leto and Artemis the archer healed him and made him glorious to look on. Meanwhile Apollo of the silver bow made a phantom in the very likeness of Aeneas, armed as he had been, and around this image Trojans and Greeks hacked at one another's shields, at the round bucklers and the light hide targets. Then Phoebus Apollo called to Ares: "Ares, Ares — butcher of men, blood-soaked stormer of walls — won't you go in and drag this man out of the fighting, this son of Tydeus, who would fight Father Zeus himself now? First he closed with the Cyprian and wounded her on the hand by the wrist, and then he sprang at me too, like something more than a man."

Apollo took his seat on the height of Pergamus, and murderous Ares went down among the Trojan ranks to rouse them, in the likeness of swift Acamas, the captain of the Thracians. He called to the sons of Priam: "Sons of Priam, kings the gods have nurtured — how long will you let the Greeks slaughter your people? Until they're fighting at the gates of Troy? A man we honored like Hector himself lies fallen — Aeneas, son of great-hearted Anchises. Come, let us pull our brave comrade out of the carnage." So he put fresh heart and fury into them all.

Then Sarpedon turned on Hector with a hard rebuke: "Hector — where has your courage gone? You used to say you could hold this city alone, without troops or allies, you and your brothers and your brothers-in-law. Well, I can't find one of them now; they slink off like dogs from a lion. It's we, your allies, who carry the fight. I came a long way to help you — from Lycia, from the eddying Xanthus, where I left my wife and my baby son and all the wealth a poor man dreams of. And still I drive my Lycians on, and stand to meet any man, though I have nothing here for the Greeks to plunder. But you stand idle, and you don't even tell your own men to hold the line and defend their wives. Take care the whole pack of you isn't caught like fish in a dragnet, and your fine city sacked and stripped. This should be on your mind night and day; you should be begging the captains of your allies to hold without flinching — and so put off the blame they lay on you."

The words stung Hector to the heart. He leaped down from his chariot in his armor, and went up and down through the army shaking his two sharp spears, urging the men to fight and rousing the terrible war cry. They turned and rallied and faced the Greeks again — and the Greeks held, massed and firm, and did not break. As wind scatters the chaff over the holy threshing floors, when men are winnowing and golden Demeter sifts the grain from the husk in the driving air, and the chaff heaps whiten — so the Greeks turned white with the dust the horses' hooves kicked up into the brazen sky, as the drivers wheeled them back into the fight. They drove their strength straight at the enemy, and furious Ares wrapped the field in darkness to help the Trojans, ranging everywhere among them; for Apollo had told him, when he saw Pallas Athena leave the battle, to put fury into the Trojans — since she had been the one defending the Greeks. And Apollo sent Aeneas himself out of his rich sanctuary and filled his chest with courage, and he took his place among his men, who were glad to see him alive and whole and full of fight. But they had no time to ask him how it had happened: there was too much to do, with the work Ares stirred up, and Strife, and Terror who never tires.

On the other side the two Ajaxes, and Odysseus, and Diomedes drove the Greeks on, fearless of the Trojan rush and roar. They stood like clouds that the son of Cronus sets on the mountaintops in still air, while the north wind sleeps with all the boisterous winds whose shrill blasts scatter the shadowing clouds — so the Greeks stood and faced the Trojans and would not run. Agamemnon went up and down among them with his orders: "Be men, my friends. Take a strong heart, and think of your good name in one another's eyes in the hard fighting. When men hold to their honor, more of them come through than are killed; but the ones who run win neither safety nor glory."

As he spoke he hurled his spear and hit a frontline man, Deicoon, son of Pergasus, a comrade of Aeneas whom the Trojans honored like a son of Priam, for he was always quick to fight up front. Agamemnon's spear struck his shield and drove clean through it, on through the belt, into the lower belly, and he fell with a crash, his armor clanging around him.

Then Aeneas killed two of the best of the Greeks, Crethon and Orsilochus. Their father was a rich man of Phere, descended from the river Alpheus, whose broad stream flows through Pylian land. The river fathered Orsilochus, lord of many men; Orsilochus fathered Diocles; and Diocles had twin sons, Crethon and Orsilochus, skilled in every kind of war. Grown to manhood, they had sailed to Ilios with the Greek fleet for the honor of the sons of Atreus, and there they died. Like two lions reared by their mother in the deep of the mountain forest, who ravage the farms and carry off the cattle and the fat sheep until they fall to a man's hand — so these two were beaten down by Aeneas, and dropped like tall pines.

Menelaus, dear to Ares, pitied them as they fell, and strode out through the front, helmed in flashing bronze, brandishing his spear — for Ares drove him on, hoping to see him killed by Aeneas. But Antilochus, son of Nestor, saw it and sprang after him, afraid the king might come to harm and waste all their effort. The two were already squaring up, spears leveled, hungry to fight, when Antilochus stepped in beside Menelaus; and bold as Aeneas was, he gave ground when he saw the two of them standing together. They dragged the bodies of Crethon and Orsilochus back to the Greek lines, laid the poor men in their comrades' arms, and turned and went on fighting up front.

There they killed Pylaemenes, a match for Ares, the leader of the great-hearted Paphlagonians.
